We analysed 14 cases of completed suicide drawn from coroner's case files in London, Southwest England and South Wales.

Our data are drawn from a qualitative study of 14 cases of completed suicide conducted in 2008e9 (Owens et al., 2009, 2011).
[page/8/2] However, as previously reported (Owens et al., 2011), our data show that, notwithstanding their desire to help, lay people are often unsure how to intervene in a suicidal crisis.

We found that the SCEs described were potentially facethreatening situations requiring face-saving strategies, which often resulted in off-record, indirect, ambiguous, humorous and euphemistic communications. Listeners frequently found it difficult to judge the meaning and intention of utterances referring to suicide. The outcome was often misunderstanding and closure of the communication, limiting the possibility of further support and referral for professional help.

[/page/3/Text/4] While SCEs can take verbal and non-verbal forms, our analysis in this paper is restricted to verbal communications of suicidal intent and ideation. These communications were reported in 11 of the 14 cases studied, as detailed in Table 1. [/page/3/Text/6] Direct communications of intent, threats or plans that made specific reference to suicide acts were reported in five cases. For example, on the day before he died one man told his aunt, "I am going to hang myself" and in the week before his suicide, another man said to his girlfriend, "If you're not going to come away with me I'm going to kill myself." [/page/3/Text/8] Direct communications of thoughts or feelings relating specifically to death or suicide were found in six cases. Thus one man who had become deeply involved in an online virtual-reality game said to his mother in the month before he died, "Life is not worth living without the game." Our data illustrate the real-life struggles of family and social network members in their attempts to make sense of communications of suicidal ideation or intent.Suicidal intent may fluctuate over the months prior to a suicidal act and while talk of suicide is relatively common, the suicidal act is relatively rare.By presenting a microanalysis of SCEs using concepts drawn from pragmatics, we have identified factors which influenced the interpretation of these critical suicide utterances.Interpretation is affected not only by the words used, but also by the background context and the pragmatic phenomena that influence meanings constructed through interaction.Difficulties in judging the sincerity of the suicide speech act were particularly common.SCEs frequently entailed threats to face for both interlocutors and the associated face-saving strategies often resulted in off-record, indirect and ambiguous communications.The cultural prohibition on talking directly about suicide led to the use of euphemisms and sometimes to a 'suicide humour' which created an interpretive incongruence between the displayed emotions and verbal references to suicidal distress.Popular assumptions about suicide talk such as 'people who talk about it don't do it' and 'I thought it was the drink talking' may also have negatively influenced the interpretation of SCEs.Although not the focus of this analysis, non-verbal communication is an important element in interpreting what is said.From these findings we suggest that the ability of significant others to recognise and intervene in the suicide process is limited by 'pragmatic failure': i.e. 'the inability to understand what is meant by what is said' (Thomas, 1983, p. 91).We also found that SCEs are sometimes closed down abruptly, leaving the significance of the event undetermined, often

[page/7/5] Our data demonstrate that SCEs can be highly face-threatening situations that are managed using face-saving tactics, including humour and off-record strategies such as strategic ambiguity and euphemistic talk. [page/7/5] Yet when the speaker bypasses face-saving using a direct commissive suicide speech act, our data show that it can be the listener who mitigates the illocutionary force of the utterance by misinterpreting its sincerity. [page/7/6] Whereas Wolk-Wasserman (1986) found that the majority of family members understood the suicidal communication but were ambivalent about helping, we found that difficulties in responding to SCEs were more frequently presented as pragmatic failures to correctly determine the meaning of the communication. [page/8/2] Lack of knowledge and confidence about intervening could make people even more reluctant to acknowledge and explore the frightening implications of what is meant by what is said. [page/8/2] Furthermore, fear of damaging a personal relationship by reading a SCE as sincere and responding inappropriately (in itself a potentially face-threatening act) may have led our participants to avoid such interpretations. [page/8/2] Mutual face-work in SCEs may sometimes be about relieving and avoiding the obligation to intervene when both interlocutors are ambivalent, fearful and unsure what to do.
